title: Meowing in Māori
bodyHtml:
Māori is a language spoken by around 50,000 people in New Zealand. Below are some sentences in Māori and their English translations. It may be helpful to know that ng and wh are consonants, and that the mark ̄ denotes a long vowel.

Kāhore au i te kite i a koe.
I do not see you.
Kua kite koe i a ia.
You have seen her.
Kei te haere tāu ngeru ki ngā whare.
Your cat goes to the houses.
Kāhore ngā tāne kia haere ki tōu whare.
The men have not gone to your house.
Kei te kite tōku matua tāne i āu ngeru.
My father sees your cats.
Kua kite au i tētahi whare.
I have seen a house.
Kei te haere āku ngeru ki tāna tāne.
My cats go to her husband.
Kāhore koe kia kōrero ki ahau.
You have not spoken to me.
Kāhore tāku tāne i te haere ki te wahine.
My husband does not go to the woman.
Kua kite te ngeru i ōna whare.
The cat has seen her houses.
Kāhore tāku tamawahine kia kōrero ki āku tamatāne.
My daughter has not spoken to my sons.

questions.promptHtml: Kei te kite au i ētahi wahine.
Kua haere ia ki te whare.
questions.answerKey: She has gone to the house.
acceptedVariants: He has gone to the house.

questions.promptHtml: Kāhore āna ngeru kia kite i ōku whare.
questions.answerKey: Her cats have not seen my houses.
acceptedVariants: His cats have not seen my houses.

questions.promptHtml: Kei te kōrero tōu matua wahine ki a ia.
I have not seen your houses.
questions.answerKey: Kāhore au kia kite i ōu whare.
Kua kite ētahi tāne i ahau.

questions.promptHtml: Her parents go to my house.
questions.answerKey: Kei te haere ōna matua ki tōku whare.

questions.promptHtml: Your wife has spoken to you.
questions.answerKey: Kua kōrero tāu wahine ki a koe.

hints.text: Sort the eleven sentences by their first word. Kei te, Kua and Kāhore are doing different jobs. Two of them mark tense; the third marks negation and changes what comes after it.

Word order is not the same in positive and negative sentences. In positive sentences the tense marker comes first and the verb follows immediately. In negatives, Kāhore comes first, then the subject, and only then a marker plus the verb. Also look closely at the possessive words: tāku, tōku, āku, ōku differ along two axes at once.

Worked example: possession. Compare tōku matua (my father) with āku ngeru (my cats) and ōna whare (her houses). The initial t- marks a single possessed thing and its absence marks plural. The vowel a or o marks the class of the possessed noun: a for spouses, children and the cat, o for parents and houses. The final piece is the possessor: -ku my, -u your, -na her. Build the rest from that.

explanationHtml:
Māori marks tense, negation and possession with small particles that all sit before the noun or verb they modify. Below, S is subject, V is verb, O is object or recipient.

Sentence structure

Positive: Kei te (present) or Kua (past) + V + S + i (direct object) or ki (directional) + a before pronouns + O.

Negative: Kāhore + S + i te (present) or kia (past) + V + i or ki + a + O.

The subject moves in front of the verb under negation. Note also that a au contracts to ahau.

Articles

singularplural
definite (the)tengā
indefinite (a, some)tētahiētahi

Possession

A possessive word is built from three pieces:

  • Number of the thing possessed — t- for one, nothing for many.
  • Class of the thing possessed — ā- for spouses, children and the cat; ō- for parents and the house.
  • Possessor — ku my, u your, na her or his.

So tōku whare is my house (one, o-class, first person) and āku ngeru is my cats (many, a-class, first person). The a/o split is a genuine grammatical class, not a rule about ownership you can guess from English.

Family terms

matua is a parent, so matua wahine is parent-woman, a mother, and matua tāne is a father. tamawahine is a daughter and tamatāne a son. A possessive particle plus tāne or wahine gives husband or wife — āku tāne is literally my man.

These sentences are graded by comparing meaning rather than exact wording, since English allows several natural phrasings. Note that ia does not mark gender, so he and she are both correct translations.
